title: PARLIAMENT QUESTION: DOMESTIC SELF-SUFFICIENCY IN CRITICAL MEDICAL RADIOISOTOPE SUPPLY
body_text:
Molybdenum-99 (Mo-99), Iodine-131(I-131) and Lutetium-177 (Lu-177) are the most important reactor-produced medical radioisotopes, accounting for nearly 90% of all Nuclear Medicine applications. Owing to their relatively short half-lives, these medical radioisotopes are produced at regular intervals, typically on a weekly or fortnightly basis in the Dhruva reactor, Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC).
The total activity of 99 Mo, 131 I and 177 Lu based radiopharmaceutical products produced and supplied during the past five years is detailed below.
Radioisotope Production capacity (Ci) Production Data (Ci) 2021- 22 2022- 23 2023- 24 2024- 25 2025- 26 Lu-177 50 Ci/batch 473 532 684 681 976 99Mo-99mTc 50 Ci/week 662 693 268 283 550 I-131 50 Ci/week 749 813 710 623 770
During maintenance shutdown of reactor/radiochemical processing facility or non-availability due to technical reasons, these radioisotopes are procured through imports from overseas producers for production and supply of radiopharmaceuticals to nuclear medicine centres.
The details of the medical radioisotopes imported during such periods, along with the quantities imported, are summarized in the Table below.
Radio-isotope Imported Quantities and Country of Origin(Curies) 2021-22 2022-23 2023-24 2024-25 2025-26 Lu-177 - - - 10 Ci (Russia) 136 Ci (Russia) Mo-99 460 Ci Australia, Russia 430 Ci Australia, Russia 30 Ci Egypt, Russia 230 Ci Egypt, Russia 516 Ci Belgium, Russia I-131 219 Ci Poland, South Africa - - 174 Ci Poland, South Africa 421 Ci Russia,    South Africa, Belgium
While Board of Radiation & Isotope Technology (BRIT) a constituent unit under Department of Atomic Energy has been able to supply the confirmed orders to an extent of ~ 90 % in conditions of normal operations, there have been shortfalls due to unforeseen shutdown of reactor/radiochemical processing facilities due to technical reasons and non-availability of imported backup supplies during such contingencies.
The details of supply shortfalls during the past five years are presented below :
Radioisotope Short supply/Cancellation 2021-22 2022-23 2023-24 2024-25 2025-26 Mo-99 (52 batches/annum) 2 batches 1 batch 13 batches 19 batches Nil I-131 (52 batches/annum) 1 batch Nil 4 batches 10 batches 3 batches Lu-177 (52 batches/annum) Nil 2 batches 2 batches 7 batches batches
Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) a Research and Development unit under Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) has obtained administrative and financial sanction to the project “Engineering and Construction of Isotope Production Reactor”. It is expected that production is likely to start around 2035 with 0.5 MCi(million Curie) radio-isotope production capacity.
This information was given by Union Minister of State for Prime Minister’s office and Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions, Atomic Energy and Space, Dr. Jitendra Singh, in a written reply in the Lok Sabha today.

enrichment.summary: In a written Lok Sabha reply, the Department of Atomic Energy detailed India's production and import of three key medical radioisotopes—Molybdenum-99, Iodine-131, and Lutetium-177—used in nearly 90% of nuclear medicine applications. These are produced at the Dhruva reactor at BARC and supplied via the Board of Radiation & Isotope Technology (BRIT), with BRIT meeting about 90% of confirmed orders under normal conditions, though shortfalls occurred during reactor/facility shutdowns necessitating imports from countries like Russia, Australia, Belgium, Egypt, Poland and South Africa. BARC has now received sanction for a new 'Isotope Production Reactor' project, expected to start production around 2035 with a capacity of 0.5 million Curies, aimed at boosting self-sufficiency.
enrichment.context:
Medical radioisotopes like Mo-99 (used via its decay product Technetium-99m for diagnostic imaging), I-131 (used in thyroid disorder treatment), and Lu-177 (used in targeted cancer therapy) are critical to India's nuclear medicine and oncology infrastructure. Because these isotopes have short half-lives, they cannot be stockpiled and must be produced continuously in research reactors, making India's near-total reliance on a single ageing reactor—Dhruva, commissioned in 1985—a strategic vulnerability. Any unplanned shutdown of Dhruva or its associated radiochemical processing facilities disrupts supply chains for hospitals nationwide, forcing costly and time-sensitive imports.

This issue fits into the broader debate on India's Atmanirbhar Bharat push in strategic and healthcare-linked technologies, and highlights gaps in domestic nuclear infrastructure for civilian applications beyond power generation. The sanctioned 'Isotope Production Reactor' project signals a long-term response to this vulnerability, though its 2035 timeline underscores the lag between policy sanction and operational self-reliance. The Department of Atomic Energy and its units—BARC (R&D) and BRIT (production/distribution)—play complementary roles in India's nuclear medicine ecosystem, and this reply provides useful data-driven insight into how import dependency fluctuates with domestic production reliability.

prelims_questions.question: Which of the following reactor-produced radioisotopes are primarily used in nuclear medicine applications in India, as highlighted in a recent Department of Atomic Energy reply in Parliament?
prelims_questions.explanation: The release specifies Mo-99, I-131, and Lu-177 as the most important reactor-produced medical radioisotopes, accounting for nearly 90% of nuclear medicine applications in India.

prelims_questions.question: The Board of Radiation & Isotope Technology (BRIT), mentioned in the context of medical radioisotope supply, functions under which body?
options: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
prelims_questions.explanation: BRIT is described in the release as a constituent unit under the Department of Atomic Energy responsible for supplying radiopharmaceuticals.
